content: The text provided appears to be a list of references from various studies, articles, and guidelines related to Ebola virus disease, infection prevention, personal protective equipment (PPE), and related topics. 1. In 2015, a study conducted in N’Zérékoré, Guinea, examined individuals in close proximity to confirmed Ebola patients. The findings were published in PLoS One in 2017. 2. Brainard et al. conducted a systematic review on the presence and persistence of Ebola and Marburg viruses in patients and survivors. This review was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2016. 3. Jones and Brosseau explored the aerosol transmission of infectious diseases, with their findings published in the Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine in 2015. 4. Lalle et al. investigated pulmonary involvement during Ebola virus disease, with their study published in the journal Viruses in 2019. 5. Mekibib and Ariën reviewed the aerosol transmission of filoviruses, with their findings published in Viruses in 2016. 6. Osterholm et al. discussed the known and unknown aspects of Ebola virus transmission, while Vetter et al. reviewed evidence on Ebola virus shedding and transmission. Both studies emphasized the need for further research. 7. Passi provided a brief review and updates on Ebola virus disease as a bioterrorism threat, highlighting its potential risks to human health. 8. Leffel and Reed examined the potential of Marburg and Ebola viruses as aerosol threats, with their findings published in Biosecurity and Bioterrorism in 2004. 9. De La Vega et al. studied key infectivity parameters in the transmission of the Ebola virus Makona strain in macaques. 10. Piercy et al. investigated the survival of filoviruses in various environments, including liquids, solid substrates, and dynamic aerosols. 11. Fischer et al. compared the aerosol stability of two strains of Zaire ebolavirus from the 1976 and 2013 outbreaks. 12. Subissi et al. reported on Ebola virus transmission caused by persistently infected survivors of the 2014–2016 West Africa outbreak. 13. Thorson et al. conducted a systematic review on viral persistence and sexual transmission from recovered Ebola survivors, providing evidence and recommendations. 14. Thorson et al. also studied the persistence of Ebola virus in semen among survivors in Sierra Leone, analyzing frequency, duration, and risk factors. 15. Varkey et al. documented the persistence of Ebola virus in ocular fluid during convalescence. 16. The World Health Organization (WHO) issued interim advice on the sexual transmission of Ebola virus disease in 2016 and provided clinical care guidelines for survivors. 17. WHO convened an international meeting in 2018 to address the persistence of Ebola virus RNA in semen and its public health implications. 18. Jacobs et al. reported a case of late Ebola virus relapse causing meningoencephalitis. 19. Mbala-Kingebeni et al. described Ebola virus transmission initiated by a relapse of systemic Ebola virus disease. 20. Medina-Rivera et al. synthesized evidence on the presence of Ebola virus in breast milk and the risk of mother-to-child transmission. 21. WHO published guidelines for managing pregnant and breastfeeding women in the context of Ebola virus disease in 2020. 22. WHO also released a pocket guide for the clinical management of patients with viral hemorrhagic fever for frontline health workers in 2016. 23. WHO developed a framework and toolkit for infection prevention and control (IPC) in outbreak preparedness and response at both national and healthcare facility levels. 24. Baller et al. conducted a descriptive study on nosocomial infections during the 2018–2020 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. 25. Hageman et al. reviewed IPC measures for Ebola in healthcare settings in West Africa and the United States. 26. Ousman et al. evaluated the impact of IPC bundle implementation on compliance during the Ebola outbreak in Mbandaka, Democratic Republic of the Congo. 27. Nyenswah et al. initiated a ring approach to IPC at non-Ebola healthcare facilities in Liberia in early 2015. 28. Nyenswah et al. also documented efforts to control the last known cluster of Ebola virus disease in Liberia in 2015. 29. Yamin et al. analyzed the effect of Ebola progression on transmission and control in Liberia. 30. Keïta et al. assessed the impact of IPC training on health facilities during the Ebola outbreak in Guinea. 31. Palagyi et al. synthesized literature on health system preparedness for emerging infectious diseases. 32. WHO emphasized the importance of human rights in the context of Ebola containment measures. 33. Pellecchia et al. examined the social consequences of Ebola containment measures in Liberia. 34. Richards et al. explored trust and distrust in Ebola treatment centers in Sierra Leone. 35. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) released reports on Ebola cases in Liberia and the United States in 2014. 36. Forrester et al. studied healthcare workers in an Ebola treatment unit and adjacent hospital in Liberia in 2014. 37. WHO outlined preferred product characteristics for PPE for healthcare workers responding to viral hemorrhagic fevers in tropical climates. 38. Hersi et al. reviewed the effectiveness of PPE for healthcare workers caring for patients with filovirus diseases. 39. Verbeek et al. evaluated PPE for preventing highly infectious diseases due to exposure to contaminated body fluids in healthcare staff. 40. Casanova et al. compared singleversus double-gloving on virus transfer to healthcare workers during PPE removal. 41. Suen et al. investigated self-contamination during PPE doffing by healthcare workers to prevent Ebola transmission. 42. Zamora et al. compared contamination risks between two personal protective systems. 43. Sprecher et al. called for better evidence on PPE for filovirus epidemics. 44. Korniewicz edited a comprehensive guide on infection control for advanced practice professionals. 45. Siegel et al. published the 2007 guideline for isolation precautions to prevent the transmission of infectious agents in healthcare settings. 46. Pshenichnaya and Nenadskaya reported probable nosocomial transmission of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus after aerosol-generating medical procedures in Russia. 47. Tran et al. reviewed the risk of transmission of acute respiratory infections to healthcare workers during aerosol-generating procedures. 48. Coca et al. conducted a physiological evaluation of PPE ensembles recommended for use in West Africa. 49. Coca et al. also performed a baseline evaluation of PPE using a sweating thermal manikin. 50. Grélot et al. studied moderate thermal strain in healthcare workers wearing PPE during the 2014 Ebola outbreak. 51. Poller et al. proposed a unified PPE ensemble for clinical response to high-consequence infectious diseases. 52. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control provided guidance on the safe use of PPE in treating high-consequence infectious diseases. 53. The CDC and the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) addressed the prevention of occupational latex allergy in healthcare workers.
